items.text: I feel settled in myself, regardless of how recent events have gone.
When I do something well, I take it as evidence rather than waiting for someone else to confirm it.
My sense of how well I am doing depends on what the last person to comment said about my work.
When something goes badly, I can separate the event from a verdict on who I am.
When I am criticised on something I have done, I find myself questioning whether I belong in the role.
When a meeting starts going wrong, I slow down rather than speed up.
After a setback at work, I can usually identify what I can act on within the next two days.
When I am under pressure, I lose track of what the people in the room actually need from me.
I can sit through a difficult meeting without people picking up that I am anxious.
After something has gone wrong, it tends to occupy my thinking for the rest of the day.
When I think a meeting is heading towards a poor decision, I say so before the decision is made.
When I commit to something at work, I commit to a specific deliverable by a specific date.
When I disagree with a senior colleague, I usually keep it to myself.
When something goes wrong in my work, I tell people about it before they find out themselves.
I tend to soften difficult messages to the point where the main point gets lost.
When I am shown evidence I was wrong about something at work, I update my position out loud.
In the last six months I have asked someone to tell me something about my work that was uncomfortable to hear.
When something I am doing is not working, I tend to try harder at it rather than try something different.
I have done something unfamiliar in my work in the last three months.
When I describe a weakness of mine, I tend to describe it as a fixed feature rather than something I am working on.
When a meeting goes badly, I usually know my part in why.
Before a significant meeting, I take a moment to notice what state I am in and choose what to do with it.
I am usually surprised when people tell me how I came across in a meeting.
I notice when my energy or focus has dropped before it affects how I am with other people.
The way I think I come across is usually how I come across to others.
When someone is telling me something difficult, I let them finish before I respond, even when I think I know what to say.
In a conversation, I can usually tell when the other person is troubled by something they have not said out loud.
I usually have my response ready before the other person has finished speaking.
When someone brings me a problem, I check what they want from the conversation before I start solving it.
After a difficult conversation, I find it hard to say what the other person was most worried about.
I acknowledge people I pass in the building who I have no reason to need anything from.
When I see someone I have met once before, I can usually remember something specific they told me.
The amount of attention I give people in a meeting depends on how senior they are.
I follow up with people after a conversation that mattered, even when there is no task attached.
The warmth I show senior people is greater than the warmth I show junior people.
In a conversation, my follow-up questions are usually about what the other person actually just said, rather than the topic I had in mind.
In the first minute of a conversation with someone new, I find out one thing about them that is not their job title.
In conversation, I tend to make a connection to my own experience before I have fully heard the other person's.
When I share an opinion in a discussion, I usually frame it as my view rather than as a fact.
The version of me that turns up in casual conversation is noticeably different from the version that turns up in formal meetings.
When someone disagrees with me in front of others, I respond at the same volume and pace I was using before.
When I am praised for something that involved someone else's contribution, I say so in the room where the praise is happening.
When I do not know something in a meeting, I find a way to talk around it rather than admit it.
In a meeting where I am the most senior person, I let others speak before I share my view.
I tend to be more measured in front of senior people than I am with everyone else.
I treat the most junior person in a meeting with the same quality of attention as the most senior.
There is a version of me that turns up when I am being evaluated, and a different version that turns up when I am not.
People who see me at work and people who see me outside it would describe me in the same terms.
When I am tired or distracted, my warmth and attention drop noticeably.
I invest in conversations with people who have nothing to offer me directly.

authenticityBands.label: Consistently available
authenticityBands.description: Behaviour is not conditional on status, usefulness, or familiarity. The same principle shows up across audiences, with appropriate surface adaptation.

authenticityBands.label: Broadly consistent
authenticityBands.description: Behaviour is reliable in most settings, with one or two specific contexts that narrow it.

authenticityBands.label: Selectively deployed
authenticityBands.description: Skills are real but unevenly distributed. Inner ring gets the full version. Peripheral contacts get less.

authenticityBands.label: Significantly instrumental
authenticityBands.description: Behaviour is at its strongest when it serves a purpose. The transactional logic is visible to others.

incidentally_invisible.label: The Incidentally Invisible
incidentally_invisible.tagline: Talented but overlooked. Ability is not the gap. Visibility is.

unknowingly_influential.label: The Unknowingly Influential
unknowingly_influential.tagline: Connects naturally. Undersells consistently. Influence outruns reputation.

occasionally_overconfident.label: The Occasionally Overconfident
occasionally_overconfident.tagline: Commands attention. Loses the room when warmth or restraint is the test.

courteously_charismatic.label: The Courteously Charismatic
courteously_charismatic.tagline: Competent and connected. The work is consistency. Closing the gap between best and average.
